I think we are in a position to do what could be a nice project, which will be of relevance and of interest to people within the high energy physics community. That is to do the following:

Formalise the Yukawa sector of the Standard Model Lagrangian, that is showing that given the SM higgs field, and fermionic fields, show that the only terms up to mass-dimension 4 are the Yukawa terms (and the Higgs potential).

The main motivation for this project is to give the first demonstration that these sorts of calculations can be done in lean. This will be of interest to people in the high-energy physics community because it's the same sort of calculations that go into effective potentials, which are quite a hot topic. It's also the sorts of calculations that go into beyond-the-standard-model theories when you add an extra particle to the standard model and you want to try and find all of the terms that are allowed under a given symmetry. I certainly think there's a paper that can be written on this topic.

If anyone wants to get involved in this let me know (if enough are interested we could use this thread to coordinate)! I've created an API map at Physlib#1419 which gives the main steps which need to be done. (Though this is not an invitation for people to point their favourite AI models at it, in an uncontrolled manner, as I think there are lots of design decisions to be made here).

Here the LinearOrder is really just a way of picking linearly independent elements, as you say above if you have a basis b := [b₁, b₂] you can use either b₁ * b₂ or b₂ * b₁ for the basis element on the second exterior power, the first comes from saying 1 < 2 and the second from 2 < 1. But you can also do this by rewriting the basis: if I instead have the basis b' := [b₂, b₁] the basis element on the second exterior power (using the usual order 1 < 2) is b₁' * b₂' = b₂ * b₁ and you recover the other basis. In a sense the order of the indexing set is distinct from the order of the basis. You would do this with docs#Module.Basis.reindex.

The way the basis of the exterior power/exterior algebra works is it takes any basis of the underlying space and builds a basis of the exterior algebra so you can swap the order of the basis elements and the basis elements of exterior algebra react accordingly. You can then write lemmas about how the reindexing impacts the resulting basis.

I have updated Physlib#1415 with a way of approaching this without having to refer to a basis. Thinking about it a bit, I think this might be the best approach because it seems like not relying on a basis actually gives you slightly nicer constructions. The idea is to replace, for example, coefficients with respect to a basis with linear projections. For example 

def coeff (s : Multiset FieldSpecification) : EffectivePotential →ₗ[ℂ] EffectivePotential :=
ExteriorAlgebra.liftAlternating (coeffOfVectorTuple s)

Defines the projection onto the terms which have individual components specified by the multi-set s. I've also defined the support of a V : EffectivePotential to be those multi-sets for which this coefficient is zero. You can then write, although I haven't proved yet: 

lemma eq_sum_support_coeff (V : EffectivePotential) : V = ∑ s ∈ support V, coeff s V := by
  sorry

One of the nice things about this is that it generalizes for different types of "coefficient". For example, you can define the projection onto the subspace spanned by terms with given irreducible representations in it by 

def irrepCoeff (i : Multiset Irrep) : EffectivePotential →ₗ[ℂ] EffectivePotential where
  toFun := fun V => ∑ s ∈ support V, if Multiset.map toIrrep s = i then coeff s V else 0

And terms with a given mass dimension by 

def massDimCoeff (n : ℚ) : EffectivePotential →ₗ[ℂ] EffectivePotential where
  toFun := fun V => ∑ s ∈ support V, if (s.map massDimension).sum = n then coeff s V else 0

We can then write things down as follows: 

lemma irrepCoeff_ψ_barψ_eq_zero_of_isInvariant {V : EffectivePotential} (hV : IsInvariant V) :
    irrepCoeff {Irrep.ψ, Irrep.barψ} V = 0 := by
  sorry

Which basically splits the calculation of the invariance of an effective potential and its form into a calculation of what its projection looks like in one of these irreducible representation spaces. This means we can make quite general statements about any effective potential and its terms within a given space. These spaces don't have too high a dimension and therefore should be relatively easy to prove things about generally.

Regarding the terminology in the codebase, I wanted to suggest that we might want to reconsider using the term "effective potential" for what we are building, as it might cause some confusion for incoming physicists. In standard QFT, the effective potential (such as the Coleman-Weinberg potential) specifically refers to the Legendre transform of the generating functional. It is an inherently quantum concept used to evaluate the exact vacuum structure of a theory by incorporating all quantum loop corrections (1PI diagrams).

However, what we are formalizing here is purely structural and algebraic. We are constructing the space of all possible non-derivative interaction terms—like the classical scalar potential, the Yukawa sector, and mass terms—up to mass-dimension 4 that are allowed by Lorentz and gauge symmetries.

Because of this, it might be much clearer to align our naming conventions with SMEFT (Standard Model Effective Field Theory). What we are essentially doing is mathematically classifying the operator basis for an effective Lagrangian. Referring to this structure as an "EFT operator basis" or the "non-derivative effective Lagrangian" would be much more precise. It accurately reflects the model-building and invariant theory we are formalizing, while avoiding the implication of loop-corrected quantum potentials.
